::: {#brief .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-cap-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The brief</p>
<p class="lx-case-q">Prairie City's council asks for its 2040 energy plan: what to change in buildings, cars, the industrial park and local supply, within $1,500 million of up-front spending, where a solar farm should go, and who gains and who pays.</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Hand in:</b> a plan link, a two-page plan summary with its sensitivity chart, and a stakeholder response table (your answers to the panel, in the summary).</li>
<li><b>From:</b> the <a href="sb3-city-planner.html">City Planner</a>'s engine, with 2040's plan on 2025's people, homes, weather and prices (Prairie City is fictional; its numbers are illustrative).</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> every check under the summary is in place (the budget, the sensitivity test and an answer to each objection among them), and the self-check reaches Proficient on every competence.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 150 minutes: 50 to build and test plans, 20 to site the solar farm, 50 to write the summary, 30 to check it.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Modeler version: plus <a href="m12-city-model.html">M12</a>'s notebook, about 60 minutes: run your plan's district levers in its last section.</p>
</div>
```
:::

## Write your two-page plan summary
:::

```{=html}
<div id="c3-note" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- c3-note:start -->
<ol class="lx-rn-outline"><li><b>Title and plan link:</b> the plan's link from the bench, and the date</li><li><b>Recommendation:</b> Three or four sentences: what Prairie City should do by 2040, and why.</li><li><b>The plan:</b> each choice, with its unit</li><li><b>Results:</b> each result, with its unit and boundary</li><li><b>Assumptions:</b> one sentence each</li><li><b>Sensitivity:</b> how one result moves when one input changes, and whether the plan was held fixed</li><li><b>Cost, CO₂ and the grid:</b> Two or three sentences: what the plan costs against the budget, what it cuts, and where the substations need room.</li><li><b>Who pays and who gains:</b> Two or three sentences on the household groups, with the adoption rule you assumed.</li><li><b>The solar farm's site:</b> One or two sentences: which site and why, or why no farm.</li><li><b>Your answers to the stakeholder panel:</b> One line for each stakeholder who objects: what you would change, or why you would not.</li><li><b>Limits of this analysis:</b> what the model leaves out</li></ol>
<!-- c3-note:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

:::

```{=html}
<div id="exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- c3-exemplars:start -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak summary · Developing</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Prairie City should go green with heat pumps and wind [1]. Emissions will fall a lot [2] and everyone will save money [3]. Some people objected but the plan is the best [4].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> No sizes, no shares, no budget: the council cannot check or cost it.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> By how much, on what boundary, against which year?</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> Who? The household table is a screening estimate with an adoption rule; name the groups and the numbers.</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> Each objection needs an answer: what you would change, or why you would not.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong summary · Proficient</p><p class="lx-ex-lines"><b>Recommendation:</b> switch 70% of furnaces and resistance heat to heat pumps, retrofit 10% of buildings, make 40% of cars electric with managed charging, add 30 MW of substation batteries, move the food plants' low-temperature heat to heat pumps, and contract 200 MW of wind and a 100 MW solar farm at site B [1].
<b>Budget and cost:</b> $1,222.6M up front against $1,500.0M; the city's yearly cost −$29.2M against 2025 (energy bills plus equipment as yearly payments, 2025 dollars) [2].
<b>CO₂ and the grid:</b> the city's CO₂ 2,121,410 t a year, 23% below 2025 (location-based, operating); 26 MW of substation upgrades, the suburbs the tightest [3].
<b>Who pays (screening):</b> energy burden of homes below 80% of area median income 6.1% → 6.3%, every group adopting alike; heat pumps raise winter electricity bills while cars' fuel savings sit outside the burden [4].
<b>Panel:</b> to the electric utility, low-income advocates, climate group, industrial park, farmers and rural residents: a line each on what I would change and why [5].
<b>Limits:</b> 2025's people and prices held to 2040, one substation per district, eight representative days, the household rule an assumption, jobs not yet estimated [6].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Every lever with its size: a plan the council can cost and check.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> Up front and yearly kept apart, on one boundary.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> The cut with its boundary, and where the plan needs grid room.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> The rule stated, and the estimate labelled as a screening estimate.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> Every objection answered.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> What the plan leaves out, so the council does not over-read it.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<!-- c3-exemplars:end -->
</div>
</div>

who pays and who gains named by household group, as a screening estimate.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Costs and emissions on different boundaries.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Cost and emissions on one boundary; emissions question named; who pays and who benefits named.</td><td data-l="Strong">Distributional and environmental side effects estimated with stated assumptions.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Uncertainty<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: The sensitivity chart attached; the inputs that could flip the recommendation named.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Single numbers.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Uncertainties classified; scenario or global sensitivity analysis; results as ranges.</td><td data-l="Strong">Decision-relevant uncertainty identified and its value discussed.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Realism<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: What the plan leaves out: power flow inside districts, 2025's people and prices held to 2040, the household rule an assumption, the map's site data.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Assumes announced projects exist.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Evidence status of key inputs; a 'what the analysis leaves out' list.</td><td data-l="Strong">Realism checked with a practitioner or primary documents.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Integrity<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: Every stakeholder who objects is answered fairly, with what you would change or why you would not.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Licences or credit unchecked.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Licences checked, credit and conflicts stated, stakeholders treated fairly.</td><td data-l="Strong">Data and code released with documentation where allowed.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Communication<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: Two pages the council can act on: the recommendation first, then the evidence, the panel and the limits.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Results without limits.</td><td data-l="Proficient">A two-page plan summary with the plan link, the sensitivity chart and the stakeholder response table: the recommendation first, then the evidence (budget, cost, CO₂, the substations, who pays), the panel's objections answered, the sensitivity and the limits.</td><td data-l="Strong">A briefing a decision-maker could act on without misreading.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
